title: Many schools
hookLine: Catholic thought also has Bonaventure, Scotus and many others; the Church keeps several schools

cards: After a whole block with one teacher, it's fair to wonder: is Thomas Aquinas simply what Catholics think? Is the Summa the official answer key, and everyone else a footnote?
A Catholic university library tells another story.

Next to Thomas sit Augustine, from long before; Bonaventure, a Franciscan who taught in Paris in Thomas's own time; John Duns Scotus, another Franciscan, who argued with Thomas's ideas after Thomas was gone.

teach.h: A SCHOOL IS A WAY OF THINKING.
teach.b: A school, here, isn't a building. It's a way of thinking that teachers hand down to students, generation after generation. Thomists follow Thomas.
Scotists follow Scotus. Others draw mainly on Augustine, or on Bonaventure. Each school has its favorite questions and its own instincts, its own way of putting God, the soul and the world together.

teach.h: PRAISED, BUT NOT THE ONLY ONE.
teach.b: The Church has praised Thomas very highly and recommended him to students for the priesthood. But it has not made him the only teacher.
On many questions it lets these schools disagree, out loud and in print, without naming a winner.

teach.h: ARGUE IN CLASS, SHARE THE ALTAR.
teach.b: Their students argue in classrooms and stay at the same altar. That's how Thomas wrote, too: in the Summa the other side always gets its say, stated fairly, before the answer.

A school that learned from Thomas has to be ready to listen to one that didn't. Paul saw an early version of this. In Corinth, people were lining up behind favorite teachers, one for Paul, one for Apollo.
Paul's answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the increase."
Teachers are gardeners. None of them owns the garden.

So as this block closes, look back at what Thomas gave: a boy who kept his call, an argument that states the other side, grace that completes, God holding the world now, habits that make us, a lamp that lights others, and straw next to what he saw.
One teacher, and many beside him.

how: Catholic universities and seminaries teach Thomas alongside Augustine, Bonaventure, Scotus and others, and theologians from different schools can debate open questions in print and in class.

o: the seminaries where priests study the Summa
Catholic colleges that each teach only Thomas
ways of Catholic thinking kept side by side

p: a way of thinking handed down
a Franciscan, in Paris in Thomas's time

games.q: you're a student in Corinth. your friends are lining up: one for Paul, one for Apollo. what does Paul tell you?
o: teachers plant and water, but God gives the growth.
follow whoever is the better speaker.
games.why: "I have planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the increase." no teacher owns the garden.

practice: Bring to mind a way of seeing things that isn't your usual one: a writer you'd never pick up, a friend whose instincts run the other way, a tradition in your own family you've quietly tuned out.

Don't argue with it yet; just ask what this teacher might see that you've been missing, and let one thing come. If you pray, ask God to plant, water or grow something through a voice you'd never have chosen.

wordCard.voice: Many schools. Thomists, Scotists, followers of Augustine and Bonaventure: ways of Catholic thinking the Church keeps side by side, without making any one of them the only teacher. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: many teachers. None of them owns the garden; God gives the increase. One block closes here.
